podcast.title: Inspired by Tommy Steele (Age 9)
podcast.body: A nine-year-old David Jones (who would later change his name to Bowie) was inspired to become a rock and roll star after seeing Tommy Steele perform on tour. Steele's "cocknified impression of an American singing style" is identified as a root for Bowie's own London take on Elvis. "On Steele's subsequent tour, a nine-year-old kid called David Jones, who would later change his name to Bowie, went to see him and came away inspired to become a rock and roll star."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

xref.title: 1964 British Television and Newspaper Appearance for Long Hair Rights
xref.body: In 1964, under his birth name David Jones, Bowie appeared on British television and in newspapers alongside other members of the International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments to publicly defend the right of men to have long hair. "In 1964, Bowie, who was still known as David Jones at the time, appeared on British television and also in the newspapers with a few members of this association to defend the right of a man to have long hair."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: 1964 TV Appearance - League for the Protection of Animal Filaments
xref.body: On November 12th, 1964, at the age of 17, David Jones appeared on television as a spokesman for a fictitious group called the "League for the Protection of Animal Filaments." This was a scam designed to get his friends on TV and earn about five pounds each, ostensibly supporting men with long hair. "He appeared as a spokesman for the league for the protection of animal filaments, a totally fictitious support group for men who chose to wear their hair long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early TV Appearance (November 12, 1964)
xref.body: At 17 years old, David Jones appeared on television as a spokesman for "The League for the Protection of Animal Filenet." This was a completely fictitious support group created by him and his friends for men with long hair, designed as a scam to get on TV and earn about five pounds each. "In 1964, at the age of 17, he appeared as a spokesman for the league for the protection of animal filenet, a totally fictitious support group for men who chose to wear their hair long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Record Appearance (1964)
xref.body: This group, featuring David Jones (later David Bowie), made his first ever appearance on record on June 5th, 1964. "The group was David Jones and the King Bees. That's the first time David Bowie ever appeared on record."

xref.title: Name Change to Avoid Confusion (1966)
xref.body: In 1966, David Jones changed his name to David Bowie to prevent being confused with Davey Jones, the "cute little English dude" from the popular TV show, The Monkees. "In 1966, David Jones would change his name to David Bowie to avoid being confused with Davey Jones, who was the cute little English dude on the TV show The Monkeys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Career Struggles as David Jones
xref.body: Before adopting his famous stage name, David Bowie was known by his birth name, David Jones. He began his musical career under this name and initially struggled to make an impact. "It was pretty, you know, spacious Bowie or David Jones as he was known back then, which is his real name, tried real hard to make something happen with music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for "Bowie" Name
xref.body: David Jones chose the name "Bowie" after becoming somewhat obsessed with the character Jim Bowie, played by actor Richard Widmark in the movie "The Alamo." Jim Bowie was a real-life American pioneer, soldier, smuggler, and slave trader famous during the Battle of the Alamo in Texas. "Our David Jones had just seen a movie called The Alamo. He became somewhat obsessed with the character played by actor Richard Widmark. That character's name was Jim Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments
xref.body: In November 1964, David Jones appeared on a BBC News program as the founder, president, and spokesman for this organization. Its purpose was to advocate for the social acceptance of young British men wearing long hair. "The first time anyone really heard about him was when he appeared on a BBC News program in November of 1964 as the founder, president, and spokesman for the International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Love for Little Richard
xref.body: As a young saxophone player, David Jones was a big fan of Little Richard, whose music and persona pushed the boundaries of early rock and roll. "David Jones was a young saxophone player who loved Little Richard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Name Change Motivation
xref.body: David Jones changed his name to David Bowie to avoid confusion with two other notable figures: a poet and painter of some renown in South London also named David Jones, and David Jones, the short kid who moved to America and joined the TV band The Monkees. "First, there was a poet and painter of some renowned and South London named David Jones. And then there was that short kid who moved to America and joined a TV band called The Monkeys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Name Change to David Bowie
xref.body: David Jones changed his name to David Bowie due to the existence of other notable David Joneses, including a poet/painter and Dave Jones of The Monkees. He was inspired by the character Jim Bowie, a real-life American pioneer, soldier, smuggler, and slave trader famous from the Battle of the Alamo, played by Richard Widmark in the movie "The Alamo." The correct pronunciation is "Bowie," not "Bowie." "So henceforth, David Jones began calling himself David Bowie, not Bowie, but Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Secret Recording of "The Next Day"
xref.body: Bowie managed to record his album "The Next Day" in complete secrecy over two years in the internet age, a feat considered miraculous. This was achieved through the unwavering loyalty of his associates, who were sworn to secrecy, and by Bowie living a remarkably low-key life in New York City with Iman. He was often seen walking, grocery shopping, and attending social events, but people were accustomed to his flamboyant personas and simply didn't notice "David Jones." "How could one of the most famous musicians in the history of the universe manage to record an album in total secrecy in the age of the internet? It was a miracle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Spokesman for International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments
xref.body: In the early 1960s, before achieving widespread fame, David Bowie (then David Jones) acted as a spokesman for a group called the International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments, advocating for men's right to wear long hair. "In the early 1960s, long before anybody knew who he was, Bowie was a spokesman for a group called the International League for the Preservation of Animal Filaments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
